column1: What are the other sterile technique rules?
column2:
Don't talk, laugh, sneeze, cough over sterile field. Hold hands above elbows during surgical scrub. Don't touch edge of container. Never turn back on sterile field. Never leave unattended.

All of these rules prevent airborne or contact contamination of the sterile field.

column1: What are Standard Precautions?
column2:
Used for EVERY patient in ALL settings. Assume ALL blood, body fluids, secretions, open skin, mucous membranes may contain pathogens. Use appropriate PPE, hand hygiene, safe injection practices.

Standard precautions are the FIRST tier of protection — applied universally regardless of diagnosis.

column1: What is the correct order for DONNING PPE?
column2:
GOWN → MASK → GOGGLES/Eye Shield → GLOVES. Memory trick: "Bottoms Up" — start from the bottom of the picture.

Gown first because it protects the most surface area. Gloves last because they are the final barrier.

column1: What is the correct order for DOFFING (removing) PPE?
column2:
GLOVES → GOGGLES → GOWN → MASK. Memory trick: Alphabetical order — G, G, G, M.

Gloves first because they are the most contaminated. Mask last because it protects your face/airway.

column1: What PPE and room type are required for Contact Precautions?
column2:
PPE: gloves & gown (eye protection if splashing). Room: private OR cohort with like infections. Double-bag linens, specimens. Disinfect equipment on removal.

Contact precautions prevent direct and indirect spread — the organism travels by touch, not air.

column1: Name 3 examples of infections requiring Contact Precautions.
column2:
MRSA (methicillin-resistant staph aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococcus), ESBL, C-Diff.

These are all MDROs — multidrug-resistant organisms. C-Diff also requires bleach for surfaces.

column1: What PPE and room type are required for Droplet Precautions?
column2:
PPE: surgical mask. Room: private OR cohort. Transport: patient wears surgical mask. Particles >5 microns travel within 3-6 feet.

Droplet particles are large and heavy — they fall within 3-6 feet. A surgical mask is sufficient.

column1: Name 3 examples of infections requiring Droplet Precautions.
column2:
Influenza, Pertussis (whooping cough), Meningitis, Mumps, Measles (Rubella/German measles), Strep throat.

All spread by large respiratory droplets during coughing, sneezing, talking, suctioning.

column1: What PPE and room type are required for Airborne Precautions?
column2:
PPE: N95 respirator (must be FIT TESTED; PAPR if not). Room: private NEGATIVE PRESSURE room ALONE; 6-12 air exchanges/hr; doors closed. Transport: patient wears surgical mask.

Airborne particles are tiny — they travel >6 feet. Negative pressure keeps them from escaping the room.

column1: Name 3 examples of infections requiring Airborne Precautions.
column2:
Measles (Rubeola), TB (Tuberculosis), Varicella (chickenpox)/open shingles, COVID, SARS. Memory: MTV + C SARS.

MTV + C SARS: Measles, TB, Varicella, COVID, SARS. These spread via tiny aerosolized particles.

column1: What is Protective Environment and who is it for?
column2:
Reverse isolation / Neutropenic Precautions. For IMMUNOCOMPROMISED patients to PROTECT THEM from organisms. NO fresh fruits/veggies/plants/flowers/standing water. No invasive procedures. Restrict sick visitors. Staff wear gloves, gown, mask.

Protective Environment is the OPPOSITE of other precautions — we protect the patient FROM us.

column1: List nursing interventions that promote wellness and support host defenses.
column2:
Hand hygiene before/after patient contact; soap & water at shift start/end, C-Diff, visibly soiled hands; medical & surgical asepsis; appropriate PPE; administer ordered meds; monitor V/S q4h; monitor labs daily; maintain skin integrity (T&P q2h); reduce stress/anxiety; promote immune function (diet, activity, sleep, lifestyle); encourage immunizations.

These are the nurse's tools for breaking the chain of infection and supporting the patient's own defenses.

column1: What are the 12 factors that affect skin integrity?
column2:
1. Age, 2. Impaired Mobility, 3. Nutrition, 4. Hydration, 5. Diminished Sensation, 6. Diminished Cognition, 7. Impaired Circulation, 8. Medication, 9. Moisture, 10. Fever, 11. Infection, 12. Lifestyle. Plus: existing medical conditions.

These are the risk factors assessed for every wound patient. Know all 12.

column1: How does age affect skin integrity in older adults?
column2:
Decreased sebaceous/sweat glands (dry skin), thinning subcutaneous layer, weakened bond between epidermis & dermis, slower healing, chronic disease interferes with healing.

The weakened epidermal-dermal bond makes older adults prone to skin tears even from minor friction.

column1: How does nutrition affect skin integrity?
column2:
Protein maintains/repairs/preserves intravascular volume. ALBUMIN level is key. Need adequate calories, ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), zinc, and copper for wound healing.

Low albumin = poor healing. Vitamin C and zinc are specifically needed for collagen synthesis and wound repair.

column1: How does hydration affect skin integrity?
column2:
BOTH over AND under hydration are harmful. Edema (poor microcirculation, ↓ O2/nutrients) AND dehydration (no elasticity, low blood flow) both increase risk of breakdown.

Think of skin like clay — too dry it cracks, too wet it softens and falls apart (maceration).

column1: How do medications affect skin integrity?
column2:
Can cause itching (pruritus), rashes, photosensitivity, pigmentation changes. NSAIDs and steroids inhibit healing. Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin) increase bleeding. Chemotherapy delays healing.

Corticosteroids suppress immune response and delay collagen synthesis — both impair wound healing.

column1: What is maceration and what causes it?
column2:
Softening/breakdown of skin from prolonged moisture exposure. Most common causes: incontinence and fever (sweating).

Maceration makes skin fragile and prone to breakdown. Keep skin clean and dry to prevent it.

column1: What are the 4 ways wounds are classified?
column2:
1. By skin integrity (open/closed), 2. By length of time for healing (acute/chronic), 3. By level of contamination (clean/clean-contaminated/contaminated/infected), 4. By depth (superficial/partial/full/penetrating).

You need to know all 4 classification systems and what falls under each.

column1: What defines a contaminated wound vs an infected wound?
column2:
Contaminated: open wounds, pressure ulcers, trauma, surgeries with break in asepsis. Infected: bacteria >100,000 per gram of tissue; s/s = REEDA, COCAF + pain.

Contaminated has organisms present but not yet causing infection. Infected = organism count exceeded threshold with clinical signs.

column1: What are the 4 depths of wounds?
column2:
Superficial (epidermis only), Partial thickness (epidermis + dermis), Full thickness (through dermis into subQ), Penetrating (through to underlying organs/cavity).

Depth determines healing method and risk. Full thickness wounds cannot heal by regeneration alone.

column1: What does COCAF stand for and what are the 5 drainage types?
column2:
COCAF = Color, Odor, Consistency, Amount, Frequency. Types: Serous (clear/watery = clean), Sanguineous (bright red = fresh blood), Serosanguineous (combo = new wound), Purulent (thick, odorous, white/yellow/grey = INFECTION), Purosanguineous (red-tinged pus = infection + new wound).

Purulent drainage = infection. Always document drainage using COCAF.

column1: What are the 4 types of wound healing?
column2:
1. Regenerative/Epithelial (partial thickness), 2. Primary Intention (clean, approximated edges, surgical wound — least infection risk), 3. Secondary Intention (greatest tissue loss, fills from base with granulation tissue — e.g. pressure ulcer), 4. Tertiary Intention (delayed closure — heals by secondary first, then sutured once no infection).

Primary = edges close together. Secondary = fills in from bottom. Tertiary = left open, then closed later.

column1: What are the 3 phases of wound healing and their timeframes?
column2:
1. Inflammatory/Cleansing: 1-5 days (hemostasis, scab, WBCs, macrophages). 2. Proliferative/Granulation: 5-21 days (HIGHEST infection risk, granulation tissue, epithelialization). 3. Maturation/Remodeling: 14-21 days to 3-6 months (collagen reorganized, scar tissue, ↑ tensile strength).

Highest infection risk is proliferative phase. Maturation can take months — scars continue to remodel.

column1: What happens during the inflammatory phase of wound healing?
column2:
Hemostasis: vessels constrict, platelets aggregate, clotting activates. Inflammation: edema, erythema, pain, ↑ temp, WBCs arrive, macrophages do phagocytosis, scab forms.

Inflammation is normal and necessary — it is the body cleaning the wound. Do not suppress it unnecessarily.

column1: What are the 5 complications of wound healing?
column2:
1. Hemorrhage (rapid blood loss), 2. Infection (organisms present, wound not healing), 3. Dehiscence (rupture/separation of wound layers), 4. Evisceration (total separation with protrusion of viscera — EMERGENCY), 5. Fistula Formation (abnormal passage connecting two body cavities).

Evisceration is always a surgical emergency. Cover with sterile saline-soaked towels immediately.

column1: What does REEDA stand for?
column2:
R = Redness, E = Edema, E = Ecchymosis, D = Drainage, A = Approximation. Used to assess surgical wounds.

REEDA gives a systematic framework for wound assessment. Approximation = are the edges coming together?

column1: Define a pressure injury and reactive hyperemia.
column2:
Localized injury to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence. Pressure → tissue ischemia → cell death. Can occur in as little as 2 hours. Reactive hyperemia: pressure causes pale/cool skin; when relieved → red. If redness does not disappear quickly = NONBLANCHABLE = tissue damage.

Nonblanchable redness = Stage I pressure injury. The tissue is already damaged even though skin is intact.

column1: What are the intrinsic factors for pressure injury development?
column2:
Chronic illness (diabetes, corticosteroids), impaired circulation (atherosclerosis, low BP), reduced O2 in blood (anemia, tobacco), limited mobility/sensation (stroke, SCI, nerve damage, contractures), impaired cognition (Alzheimer's, dementia), immobility, poor nutrition, edema, age, fever/sepsis.

Intrinsic = internal to the patient. These are patient health status factors you cannot always control.

column1: What are the extrinsic factors for pressure injury development?
column2:
Friction, Shearing (patient sliding down — epidermis and dermis separate), Moisture, Compression over bony prominences or under medical devices (ET tubes, casts, catheters).

Extrinsic = external/environmental factors. These ARE controllable through nursing interventions.

column1: Describe the 4 stages of pressure injuries.
column2:
Stage I: skin INTACT, nonblanchable, epidermis only. Stage II: skin OPEN, partial thickness (epidermis + dermis), red-pink, may be blister. Stage III: full thickness (epidermis + dermis + subQ), may see fascia. Stage IV: full thickness + muscle/bone/tendon/joint capsule, slough/eschar, undermining/sinus tracts.

Healing ulcers are NEVER reverse-staged. A Stage IV healing = "Stage IV: healing," not Stage III.

column1: What is the Braden Scale and what are its 6 categories?
column2:
Tool to assess skin impairment and pressure injury risk. 6 categories: Sensory Perception, Moisture, Activity, Mobility, Nutrition, Friction & Shear. LOWER score = MORE risk. ≤18 = at risk. <12 = high risk. Performed every shift/q8h.

Memory trick for categories: S-M-A-M-N-F (Some Moist Areas May Need Friction).

column1: What are the key nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries?
column2:
Inspect skin daily/q1-2h. T&P q2h. Manage moisture (incontinence care, barrier cream). Lotion & massage — DO NOT massage over bony prominences. Monitor labs/nutrition/hydration. Pressure limiting devices. Keep HOB at lowest degree consistent with condition. Totally relieve heel pressure (raise heels off bed). Use lifting devices (Hoyer lift).

Massaging over bony prominences can increase tissue damage. Always lift — never drag — patients.

column1: What are the effects and indications for heat therapy?
column2:
Effects: vasodilation, ↑ capillary permeability, ↑ cellular metabolism, ↑ inflammation. Indications: joint stiffness, contractures, low back pain. Increases blood flow → brings O2 and WBCs → aids healing. Promotes relaxation, ↓ stiffness/muscle tension.

Heat increases circulation to the area — beneficial for healing but can worsen acute bleeding/swelling.

column1: What are the effects and indications for cold therapy?
column2:
Effects: vasoconstriction, ↓ capillary permeability, ↓ cellular metabolism, slowed bacterial growth, ↓ inflammation/edema, local anesthetic effect. Indications: fractures, post-injury swelling, bleeding, sprains, strains.

Cold reduces swelling and acts as a natural analgesic. Use for ACUTE injuries, not chronic stiffness.

column1: What are the nursing interventions for heat/cold therapy?
column2:
PCP prescription required (site, type, frequency, duration). Assess site and pt's perception of temp. VS pre & post. Inspect skin every 15 min. Receptors adapt in ~15 min — warn pt NOT to change temp. Monitor carefully: extremes of age, sensory impairment, highly vascular areas, large body area, injured skin.

If patient says it "doesn't feel as hot/cold anymore" — that is receptor adaptation, NOT a sign to increase temp.

column1: What are reliable sources of drug information?
column2:
US Pharmacopeia (USP/NF), Physician's Desk Reference (PDR), package inserts, nursing drug handbooks, Medline, DailyMed, clinical pharmacist, facility policies. Google/Facebook/Instagram/TikTok are NOT reliable.

As an RN you are ethically, legally, and personally responsible for knowing what you are giving. Always use reliable sources.

column1: What information is found in a drug reference?
column2:
Description, Action, Indication for use, Interactions, Contraindications, Precautions, Side effects, Adverse reactions, Dosage and routes of administration, How to store.

Know this list — if you don't know one of these things about a drug, look it up before giving it.

column1: What are the 3 ways drugs are named?
column2:
Chemical: exact composition, rarely used in nursing (isobutylphenyl propionic acid). Generic: official/common name, NOT capitalized (ibuprofen), listed in US Pharmacopeia. Trade: brand name, CAPITALIZED, trademark symbol (Motrin, Advil).

Generic = lowercase (ibuprofen). Trade = Capitalized (Advil). RNs use generic names most often.

column1: What are the 4 ways drugs are classified?
column2:
1. Body system (where it works — cardiovascular, GI), 2. Clinical indication/therapeutic use (why it's used — antihypertensive, laxative), 3. Physiologic/chemical action (what it does — beta blocker, stool softener), 4. Prescription/non-prescription/illegal.

One drug can appear in multiple categories — e.g., Tylenol is both analgesic and antipyretic.

column1: What are all routes of administration?
column2:
Oral, Enteral (NG/G-tube), Transmucosal (sublingual/buccal), Topical (skin/instillation/inhalation), Parenteral (IV/IM/SQ/ID), Parenteral other (intraspinal/intrathecal/epidural/rectal).

Parenteral = any route that bypasses the digestive system. IV is fastest onset.

column1: What is the sublingual route and what drug uses it?
column2:
Drug held UNDER THE TONGUE. Do NOT swallow — allow to dissolve and absorb. Rapid absorption into circulation, bypasses stomach. Example: NITROGLYCERIN.

Sublingual gives the fastest oral route absorption because it goes directly into blood vessels under the tongue.

column1: What is the buccal route and what drug uses it?
column2:
Drug held against mucous membrane IN THE CHEEK. Must dissolve. Rapid absorption, bypasses stomach. Examples: liquid Roxinol (end-of-life), Methyltestosterone.

Both sublingual and buccal bypass the GI tract for rapid absorption. Do not let patient swallow either.

column1: What are the drug absorption sites from Table 2.1?
column2:
Sublingual → under tongue (Nitroglycerin). Buccal → cheek (Methyltestosterone). Oral → stomach/intestine (Ibuprofen). IM → muscle (Prochlorperazine). SubQ → under skin (Epinephrine, Insulin). IV → bloodstream (Antibiotics, antineoplastics). Topical → through skin (Nitrodisc, hydrocortisone). Rectal → rectum (Bisacodyl).

Know each drug-to-route example from this table — it is directly tested.

column1: Compare IV, IM, SQ, and ID routes.
column2:
IV: directly in vein, fastest, one stick multiple doses, risk infection/vein problems. IM: into muscle, larger volume, risk nerve damage, no damaged tissue. SQ: under skin, slower than IM, small amounts only (insulin, heparin). ID: into dermis, very small amounts, slowly absorbed (PPD, allergy testing).

Speed of absorption: IV > IM > SQ > ID. IV is nearly instant. ID is the slowest.

column1: What are the 4 concepts of pharmacokinetics (ADME)?
column2:
Absorption: drug moves from route of admin into bloodstream. Distribution: drug delivered via bloodstream to desired site. Metabolism: drug breaks down at site — PRIMARY SITE = LIVER. Excretion: drug eliminated — PRIMARY SITE = KIDNEYS.

ADME: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion. Liver metabolizes, Kidneys excrete.

column1: What factors affect drug absorption?
column2:
Route (IV fastest), Drug solubility (water soluble = faster GI absorption; lipid soluble = penetrates cells; enteric coated = delayed; time release = slow), Blood flow to area (poor supply = poor absorption), Age (older adults have ↓ stomach acid, ↓ motility, ↓ muscle/subQ tissue), Patient condition.

Older adults absorb drugs more slowly and unpredictably — monitor carefully for toxicity.

column1: Define onset of action, peak, trough, and half-life.
column2:
Onset: TIME for drug to reach effective blood level. Peak: HIGHEST concentration — draw blood 2 HOURS after dose. Trough: LOWEST concentration (next dose due) — draw 30 MINUTES BEFORE next dose. Half-life: TIME for HALF the drug to be eliminated. Therapeutic range: concentration that causes desired effect without toxicity.

Peak draw = 2 hrs after dose. Trough draw = 30 min BEFORE next dose. These timing rules are critical for accuracy.

column1: What are primary vs secondary drug effects?
column2:
Primary effects: PREDICTED, DESIRED, INTENDED (therapeutic effect). Secondary effects: ALL UNINTENDED/non-therapeutic effects — everything other than what was intended.

Any effect beyond the desired therapeutic one is a secondary effect — may be harmless or dangerous.

column1: What are the 6 types of secondary drug effects?
column2:
1. Side effects (predictable, tolerable, can continue drug), 2. Adverse reactions (harmful, unpredicted, STOP drug), 3. Toxic reactions (damages organs, can be fatal), 4. Allergic reactions (immune response — hives to anaphylaxis), 5. Idiosyncratic (unexpected/paradoxical — opposite of expected), 6. Cumulative effect (↑ response from repeated doses when metabolism < administration rate — seen in liver/kidney failure).

Idiosyncratic example: Benadryl causing hyperactivity in a child instead of drowsiness. Paradoxical = opposite of expected.

column1: What are the signs of anaphylactic allergic reaction?
column2:
Life-threatening: laryngeal/pharyngeal edema, bronchoconstriction, hypotension. May start with hives (urticaria), itching (pruritus), swelling (edema), rhinitis.

Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency requiring epinephrine immediately. Progresses from mild to life-threatening rapidly.

column1: What are the 5 types of drug interactions?
column2:
1. Agonist: 1+1=2 (desired combined effects), 2. Antagonistic: 1+1=1 (one blocks the other), 3. Synergistic: 1+1=3 (additive — greater than either alone), 4. Potentiating: A+B=AAAAAA (one greatly enhances other TO TOXICITY), 5. Incompatibilities: 1+1=0 (mixed drugs cause chemical deterioration — clear IV turns cloudy = DO NOT give).

Incompatible drugs that are mixed and administered = MEDICATION ERROR. Always check compatibility before mixing.

column1: What are the 4 components of body mechanics?
column2:
Body alignment, Balance, Coordination, Joint mobility.

All 4 work together. Proper alignment = neutral spine. Wide base of support = balance.

column1: What does the ANA (2013) say about patient lifting?
column2:
Use mechanical equipment (transfer board, lift) OR get assistance for lifting/transferring whenever possible. Do NOT rely on body mechanics alone to prevent injury.

This is a safety standard to protect both nurses and patients. "Get help" is always the right answer.

column1: What are the body mechanics rules for avoiding injury?
column2:
Proper alignment (neutral spine). Wide base of support. Avoid bending/twisting (face object, squat). Keep objects close. Raise bed to waist height. Push/slide/pull rather than lift. Smooth even movements. Use mechanical equipment. Get help!

Squat to lift — lowers center of gravity. Keep elbows bent when carrying. Never jerk or twist.

column1: What is the purpose of Range of Motion (ROM)?
column2:
Exercise and keep body in best possible physical condition when bed rest or immobility is present. Improves joint mobility, increases circulation, maintains function, prevents contractures.

ROM = maximum movement possible at a joint. Without ROM exercises, joints stiffen and muscles waste.

column1: What is the difference between AROM and PROM?
column2:
AROM (Active ROM): done BY THE PATIENT without assistance — patient independently moves joints. PROM (Passive ROM): done BY THE NURSE FOR the patient because they CANNOT do it themselves — prevents complications of disuse, promotes joint mobility, prevents contractures/atrophy.

Active = patient does it. Passive = nurse does it FOR the patient. Both are valuable.

column1: What are the 8 factors affecting activity and mobility?
column2:
1. Developmental stage (age), 2. Cognitive status, 3. Nutrition (low albumin = muscle loss), 4. Lifestyle (sedentary), 5. Stress (cortisol/adrenaline = muscle tension, fatigue), 6. Environmental factors, 7. Diseases/abnormalities, 8. Respiratory/circulatory disorders, fatigue, bed rest.

Older adults should get 30 min/day including resistance and balance training to prevent falls.

column1: What are the musculoskeletal complications of immobility?
column2:
Balance problems, loss of endurance, muscle atrophy (10% strength loss PER WEEK), wasting of leg muscles, joint stiffness, ↓ stability, joint contractures (flexors pull joints → ankylosis), disuse osteoporosis (bone releases calcium), hypercalcemia.

Muscle atrophy begins within days. 10% per week is the key number for muscle strength loss.

column1: What are the respiratory complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complications: ↓ lung expansion, respiratory muscle weakness, pooling of secretions, atelectasis, pneumonia. Interventions: orthopneic position, T&P q2h, cough & deep breathe, incentive spirometer, increase fluids to liquefy secretions.

Pooled secretions block airways → atelectasis → pneumonia. This is why we get immobile patients breathing deeply.

column1: What are the cardiovascular complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complications: edema, venous stasis, DVT, orthostatic hypotension, blood pooling, ↑ HR, ↓ cardiac reserve. Interventions: DVT prophylaxis, ROM, monitor HR. Why: muscle contraction pumps blood back to heart — immobility stops this.

Stasis of blood = edema = thrombus. Prevent DVT before it becomes a PE.

column1: What are the metabolic complications of immobility?
column2:
Decreased serum albumin → edema. Decreased protein stores → muscle loss. Calcium leaves bones → hypercalcemia, osteoporosis, renal calculi, calcium deposits in joints. Decreased BMR. ↓ Protein/glycogen synthesis, ↑ fat stores.

Hypercalcemia from immobility can lead to kidney stones. Weight-bearing exercise is key for bone density.

column1: What are the GI complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complications: anorexia (↓ appetite/digestion from ↓ metabolic rate), constipation (↓ peristalsis, gas), PARALYTIC ILEUS (cessation of peristalsis). Interventions: small frequent meals, high calorie/protein diet, monitor weight, ↑ fluids, ↑ fiber, monitor BMs, stool softeners.

Paralytic ileus = peristalsis stops completely. Listen for bowel sounds — their absence is a red flag.

column1: What are the GU complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complications: renal calculi, ↓ urinary output, urinary stasis, UTIs, urinary retention (↓ bladder tone). Why: supine position inhibits drainage, urine stagnates, ↑ calcium → stone formation. Interventions: monitor I&O, encourage/increase fluids, sit upright or OOB to urinate.

Stagnant urine = perfect environment for bacteria + calcium stone formation.

column1: What are the integumentary complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complication: Pressure injuries (pressure over bony prominences → ↓ circulation → tissue hypoxia → tissue damage). Interventions: T&P q2h, pressure-reducing devices, trapeze, turn sheets, friction-reducing devices, keep incontinent skin clean and dry.

Pressure injuries can develop in as little as 2 hours — this is why T&P q2h is the standard.

column1: What are the psychosocial complications of immobility and interventions?
column2:
Complications: depression, behavioral changes, sleep disturbances, isolation, sensory deprivation, ↑ dependence, moodiness/anxiety/hostility, ↓ concentration/recall, reduced self-care ability. Interventions: provide socialization, place with others, social worker consult, activities.

Immobility affects the whole person — not just the body. Emotional and cognitive decline are real complications.

column1: What are the 3 phases of perioperative nursing and when does each begin/end?
column2:
Preoperative: client's decision to have surgery → enters OR. Intraoperative: enters operating suite → admitted to PACU. Postoperative: enters PACU → healed from procedure (2 parts: recovery from anesthesia in PACU, then recovery from surgery on surgical unit).

Know the exact start and end points for each phase — these are commonly tested.

column1: What are the 4 ways surgeries are classified?
column2:
1. By body system, 2. By purpose, 3. By degree of urgency, 4. By degree of risk.

Each classification system has its own categories. Know examples for each.

column1: What are the 7 surgical purposes?
column2:
Ablative (removal — appendectomy), Diagnostic (confirm dx — biopsy), Palliative (relieves symptoms, not curative — nerve root destruction), Reconstructive (restores function — rotator cuff), Cosmetic (appearance — facelift), Transplant (replaces organ), Procurement (organ harvested for another patient).

Palliative does NOT cure — it only relieves suffering. Procurement = organ donation surgery.

column1: What are the 3 degrees of urgency in surgery?
column2:
Elective: recommended, NOT time-sensitive, pt may delay (rotator cuff, liposuction). Urgent: within 24-48 hours to alleviate/restore (cancerous breast removal, internal fracture fixation). Emergency: ASAP to preserve life/function (trauma, organ rupture, hemorrhage, bowel perforation).

Urgency determines how quickly prep must happen. Emergency = no time for full pre-op workup.

column1: What is major vs minor surgery?
column2:
Major: high risk, significant blood loss, prolonged/complicated, vital organs, high postop complications (CABG, colon resection, nephrectomy). Minor: low risk, often outpatient, few complications (arthroscopy, breast biopsy, endoscopy, inguinal hernia repair).

Risk depends on: client condition, type of surgery, anesthesia used, pre-existing conditions.

column1: What are the key factors contributing to surgical risk?
column2:
Age (very young/very old), type of wound, pre-existing conditions (infections, cardiac, COPD, diabetes, liver/kidney disease), mental status, medications, personal habits (smoking, alcohol), allergies (antibiotics, analgesics, latex, anesthesia, shellfish).

Allergies to shellfish/iodine are relevant because many contrast dyes used in surgery contain iodine.

column1: How do medications increase surgical risk? Give examples.
column2:
Anticoagulants (↑ bleeding), Antihypertensives (↑ hypotension, bradycardia with anesthesia), Aspirin (↑ bleeding), Corticosteroids (delay healing, ↑ infection), Opioids (↑ resp depression), Antibiotics (mask infections, potentiate anesthetics), Antidysrhythmics (impair cardiac during anesthesia), Diuretics (alter F/E — especially K+), NSAIDs (↑ bleeding), Tranquilizers (↑ resp depression).

Always review ALL medications — including OTC and herbals — before surgery.

column1: What is the most common surgical complication in older adults?
column2:
DELIRIUM. Predisposing factors: older age, functional disabilities, many coexisting conditions, poor vision/hearing, cognitive impairment, alcohol abuse.

Delirium in older surgical patients is NOT normal confusion — it is a complication that must be identified and treated.

column1: What are the preoperative nursing responsibilities?
column2:
History & physical, Lab & diagnostic tests, Pre-op teaching, Informed consent, Prepare client physically & mentally.

All 5 must be completed before surgery. The nurse coordinates — the surgeon explains the procedure.

column1: What does the pre-op history & physical include?
column2:
History: health history, allergies, medications, mental status, understanding of surgery. Physical: head-to-toe assessment, respiratory status, VS, risk for thrombophlebitis (immobility, dehydration, long surgeries, heart failure, varicose veins, pregnant/recent childbirth, smoker).

ALL patients must be assessed for thrombophlebitis risk pre-op.

column1: What pre-op lab/diagnostic tests are ordered and why?
column2:
CBC (anemia, WBC, clotting), Urinalysis (UTI, diabetes, pregnancy), CMP (electrolytes, liver, albumin, BUN/creatinine), Fasting Blood Sugar (DM), Blood type & crossmatch (transfusion), Serum Electrolytes (CV/renal/F&E), ECG (cardiac dysrhythmias), CXR (pulmonary disease, heart size), Serum Albumin (nutrition).

Each test has a specific purpose tied to surgical risk. Know what each test detects.

column1: What are the physical preparation steps before surgery?
column2:
Maintain normothermia, NPO status (after midnight/6-8 hrs preop), skin prep (chlorhexidine), bowel prep, last void or catheterization, pre-op meds, status of routine meds. REMOVE: dentures, artificial limbs, contacts, wigs, jewelry, nail polish, eyeglasses, hearing aids. Apply anti-embolism stockings/SCDs.

Label any kept items (eyeglasses, hearing aids). Nail polish is removed to allow pulse ox monitoring.

column1: What does pre-op teaching include?
column2:
Pain management (priority), Coughing & deep breathing (prevents atelectasis/pneumonia), Incentive spirometer (INSPIRATION — opens alveoli), Splinting (folded blanket/pillow — ↓ pain, ↓ dehiscence risk), Leg exercises (ankle circles, knee bends — prevent DVT), Anti-embolism stockings, Sequential compression devices, Post-op dressings/equipment.

Pre-op teaching is done before surgery so the patient knows what to expect and can practice.

column1: What are the pre-op medications and their purposes?
column2:
Opioids (morphine, meperidine, fentanyl — pain/sedation), Antibiotics (ampicillin, vancomycin, cefazolin — reduce microbial burden), Midazolam/VERSED (anxiolytic, amnesiac, benzodiazepine), Propofol/DIPRIVAN (moderate sedation), Atropine (anticholinergic — reduces secretions, prevents aspiration), Ondansetron (antiemetic — prevents vomiting → aspiration pneumonia).

Atropine dries up secretions to reduce aspiration risk. Ondansetron prevents N&V that could cause aspiration.

column1: What are the roles of the surgeon and nurse in informed consent?
column2:
SURGEON: explains procedure/risks/benefits, obtains signature, determines competence. NURSE: verifies consent signed & witnessed, witnesses signing, verifies it is in medical record. RN does NOT explain the procedure. If pt doesn't understand → STOP, notify surgeon, DO NOT send to OR.

The RN's role is verification and witnessing — NOT explanation. Never send a patient to the OR who does not understand their surgery.

column1: What is the Universal Protocol and Time Out?
column2:
Universal Protocol includes site marking and Time Out. Site marking: practitioner marks, nurse VERIFIES, involve patient. Time Out: occurs INTRAOPERATIVELY, all team members pause IMMEDIATELY before procedure, each member identifies: PATIENT, SITE, PROCEDURE.

Time Out prevents wrong-patient, wrong-site, wrong-procedure errors. Every team member must participate.

column1: What is the role of the circulating nurse vs the scrub nurse?
column2:
Circulating nurse: CLEAN team, does NOT enter sterile field, client advocate, coordinator, monitors pt and sterile field, documents, handles specimens. Scrub nurse: STERILE team, sets up sterile field, prepares instruments, passes to surgeon, maintains sterile field integrity — BOSS of sterile field.

Circulating = clean, moves around room. Scrub = sterile, stays at the sterile field.

column1: What are the 4 types of anesthesia?
column2:
Local: loss of pain at site only, minor procedures, injected or topical (lidocaine, benzocaine). Moderate/Conscious Sedation: sedation + analgesia, pt aware but sleepy, rapid recovery (endoscopies). Regional: interrupts nerve impulses to area, pt awake (nerve blocks, spinal, epidural). General: rapid unconsciousness via inhaled/IV meds, requires INTUBATION, risk of stroke/death/MI.

Regional = awake but numb. General = completely unconscious and requires airway management.

column1: What is the PACU priority assessment (ABCs)?
column2:
1. Airway (patent? chest rising? if unconscious → side-lying), 2. Breathing (RR, lung sounds, skin color, pulse ox >90%), 3. Circulation (BP, pulse, drainage on dressing, peripheral pulses, hematoma), 4. Nausea/Pain (vomiting can obstruct airway).

Phase 1 PACU = highest risk for respiratory and cardiac compromise. ABC assessment is the priority.

column1: What are the criteria for evidence of recovery from anesthesia in the PACU?
column2:
Airway: maintains patent airway, can cough/expectorate. LOC: conscious, easily reoriented. VS: stable. Mobility/sensation: moves all extremities, spinal/epidural worn off. Fluid balance: urinating ≥30 mL/hr. Dressings: dry and intact or drainage appropriate for procedure.

Urinating ≥30 mL/hr is the key indicator of adequate renal perfusion and fluid balance after anesthesia.

column1: What are the VS assessment intervals when a patient arrives from PACU to the surgical floor?
column2:
On arrival: IMMEDIATELY. Then: q15 min x 1 hour, q30 min x 2 hours, q1 hour x 4 hours, then q4 hours. Assessment = full physical head-to-toe including all lines, tubes, dressings, I&O.

These intervals reflect the highest monitoring intensity immediately post-op, tapering as the patient stabilizes.

column1: What is progressive ambulation and what is the sequence?
column2:
Post-op ambulation sequence: 1. Sit and dangle feet at bedside (assess for orthostatic hypotension/dizziness/pain), 2. Sit in chair (OOB), 3. Walk in room, 4. Walk in hallway. Must be assisted. Check VS stable before getting up.

Low BP on standing = orthostatic hypotension → patient will faint. Always check VS and have patient dangle first.

column1: What is the post-op diet progression order?
column2:
NPO → Clear Liquids → Full Liquids → Soft Diet → Prescribed/Regular diet.

Progress only when each stage is tolerated. Must verify 6 things before starting any diet.

column1: What foods are included in Clear Liquids?
column2:
Black coffee, plain tea, carbonated drinks, bouillon/broth, clear fruit juice, popsicle, gelatin, hard candy.

Clear liquids = no solids, no dairy, nothing you cannot see through. Think: see-through and non-dairy.

column1: What foods are included in Full Liquids?
column2:
All clear liquids PLUS: milk/dairy, vegetable juices, cream, butter, yogurt, puddings, custard, cream of wheat, ice cream, sherbet.

Full liquids = everything liquid or that melts at room temperature. Dairy is now allowed.

column1: What 6 things must be assessed before starting a post-op diet?
column2:
1. HCP orders, 2. LOC (never feed unconscious pt), 3. Can they swallow? (if can't swallow saliva, can't swallow food), 4. Do they have a gag reflex? (without gag → aspirate), 5. Is GI tract functioning? (bowel sounds, belching, passing flatus), 6. Nausea? Vomiting?

All 6 must be checked EVERY time before advancing diet. Missing any one of these risks aspiration.

column1: What are the 3 surgical drains and how does each work?
column2:
Penrose: flat flexible latex tube, not sutured, placed in wound bed, measure exposed length each assessment. Jackson-Pratt (JP): suction drain, must COMPRESS to activate suction, empty at ½ full. Hemovac: suction drain, must compress for suction, empty at intervals.

JP and Hemovac both use suction — if full, suction fails. Never wait until completely full. ALWAYS maintain drains BELOW incision site.

column1: What does ongoing drain assessment include?
column2:
Is it draining? COCAF — color/amount changed? Stopped? Why? What does the drain site look like? REEDA? Pain? Report any significant change to provider. If no drainage → may be occluded, remove kinks. MAINTAIN drains BELOW incision site.

A drain that suddenly stops draining may be kinked or occluded — investigate before assuming the wound stopped draining.

column1: What does REEDA stand for and what is it used for?
column2:
R = Redness, E = Edema, E = Ecchymosis, D = Drainage, A = Approximation. Used to assess surgical wounds post-op. Surgeon changes the FIRST dressing.

Approximation = are wound edges coming together? If not → dehiscence risk. Count sutures/staples/steri-strips.

column1: What is dehiscence and what are the nursing interventions?
column2:
Separation of ONE OR MORE layers of wound (not total). Causes: poor nutrition, obesity, strain on suture line, infection. Interventions: dry sterile dressing, HOB 20 degrees + knees flexed, apply BINDER (to prevent evisceration), notify provider, monitor.

Dehiscence = partial separation. Binder prevents it from progressing to evisceration. HOB and knees flexed reduce tension on incision.

column1: What is evisceration and what are the nursing interventions?
column2:
TOTAL separation of wound layers with internal viscera PROTRUDING through. Surgical EMERGENCY. Interventions: cover with STERILE TOWELS soaked in STERILE SALINE, bedrest with KNEES BENT, HOB 20 degrees, DO NOT put a binder on, notify surgeon, PREP FOR SURGERY.

NO binder with evisceration — organs are already out, binder would compress them. Moist sterile towels prevent drying and contamination.

column1: What are the signs and interventions for post-op hemorrhage?
column2:
Risk greatest: first 24-48 hours. External: dressing saturated bright red blood, ↑ blood in drains, dependent drainage (check UNDER pt). Internal: ↑ pain, edema/swelling around incision, hematoma, ecchymosis. VS both: TACHYCARDIA + FALLING BP (hypotension). Interventions: monitor VS, assess dressing/drainage/wound/drains.

If dressing has blood — ALWAYS check under the patient for pooled dependent drainage. Internal bleed is harder to detect.

column1: What are the signs of post-op infection and when do they appear?
column2:
S/S: swelling, redness, heat, pain, fever >100.4°F, ↑ HR, foul/purulent drainage. Clean wound: s/s NOT until 4th-5th post-op day. Contaminated/traumatic wound: s/s within 2-3 days. Interventions: monitor s/s, VS, sterile technique for dressing changes, hand hygiene, culture if ordered.

The 4th-5th day rule for clean wounds is high-yield. Earlier signs = think contaminated wound.

column1: What are the signs and treatment of thrombophlebitis vs pulmonary embolism?
column2:
Thrombophlebitis: blood clot + inflammation in leg vein; caused by blood stasis; s/s: leg red, hot, edematous, cramping. Treatment: immobilize limb, may have heparin. PE: clot breaks off, travels to lungs; s/s: SUDDEN dyspnea, SOB, chest pain, hypotension, tachycardia, ↓ SaO2, cyanosis. Prevention: PREVENT DVT.

PE is life-threatening. Sudden dyspnea after surgery = think PE until proven otherwise.

column1: What is post-op pneumonia and its signs?
column2:
Inflammation of alveoli from hypoventilation secondary to anesthesia and opioids, poor cough effort. Airways fill with solid material. S/S: productive cough (blood-tinged or purulent), fever, chills, ↑ WBC, ↓/absent lung sounds, low SaO2, dyspnea, pleural pain, tachycardia/tachypnea, malaise.

Prevent with incentive spirometer, C&DB, early ambulation, and adequate pain control so pt can breathe deeply.

column1: What is aspiration pneumonia and why does it occur post-op?
column2:
Airway inflammation from inhaling gastric secretions (HCl) due to absent gag reflex from anesthesia. S/S: cough, fever, ↑ WBC, ↓ breath sounds, ↓ SaO2, tachypnea, blood-tinged sputum. Prevention: NPO ≥8 hrs preop, NPO postop until GI motility returns, side-lying if sedated, check gag reflex before diet.

This is WHY we check LOC, swallow ability, gag reflex, and bowel sounds before starting any diet.

column1: What is post-op nausea and vomiting (N&V) and how is it managed?
column2:
Related to pain, anxiety, anesthesia, or oral intake before peristalsis returns. Risks: aspiration pneumonia, dehiscence (strain on suture line). Interventions: keep NPO, assess for return of bowel sounds, administer antiemetic as ordered (ondansetron).

Vomiting strains the incision and risks aspiration. Ondansetron (anti-emetic) is on the Unit 1 drug list.

column1: What are the 3 ways pain is classified?
column2:
1. By ORIGIN: cutaneous (skin/subQ), deep somatic (ligaments/bone/tendons), visceral (organs), radiating/referred, phantom (missing limb), psychogenic (no physical cause). 2. By CAUSE: nociceptive (tissue damage), neuropathic (nerve injury — burning/numbness/pins & needles). 3. By DURATION: acute (rapid onset, up to 6 months), chronic (3-6+ months, interferes with ADLs), intractable (chronic, highly resistant to relief, needs multiple methods).

All 3 classification systems can be tested independently. Phantom pain is real — the brain perceives it.

column1: What are the 4 pain assessment scales and when to use each?
column2:
NRS (0-10): adults who can count — 0=no pain, 10=worst. VAS: 10-cm line, simple/quick but may be abstract. Wong-Baker FACES: children >3 yrs, adults with communication/cognitive impairments — face illustrations, no numbers needed. FLACC (<4 yrs or nonverbal): Face/Legs/Activity/Cry/Consolability, each 0-2, for 2 months-7 years OR anyone unable to communicate.

Key ages: FLACC <4 yrs, Wong-Baker >3 yrs. Absence of cues does NOT mean no pain — especially in cognitively impaired.

column1: Name the 16 non-pharmacologic pain interventions.
column2:
1. Positioning/posture, 2. Education/anticipatory guidance, 3. Touch/massage (back rub), 4. Relaxation/distraction/music/pet therapy, 5. Meditation/guided imagery, 6. Aromatherapy, 7. Acupuncture/acupressure, 8. TENS, 9. PENS, 10. Heat/cold treatment, 11. Contralateral stimulation, 12. Progressive muscle relaxation, 13. Hypnosis, 14. Journaling, 15. Humor, 16. Oral sucrose. Use IN CONJUNCTION with medications.

These do NOT replace medications — they supplement them. Used together, pain management is most effective.

column1: What are the side effects of opioids and the reversal agent?
column2:
Side effects: respiratory depression, sedation, nausea, vomiting, constipation, urinary retention, facial flushing, itching. If RR <10: STOP opioids, give NALOXONE (NARCAN). Always assess RR, O2 sat, and LOC before AND after administering opioids.

Respiratory depression is the most dangerous opioid side effect. Narcan reverses all opioid effects including pain relief.

column1: What are the 2 PCA modes and the nursing responsibilities?
column2:
Mode 1: patient pushes button for dose. Mode 2: patient pushes button PLUS continuous basal dose. Nursing: verify order/allergies/settings with 2 RNs, continuous pulse oximetry, NEVER push button for pt, never allow family to push button, educate pt (call before OOB, use before activity).

NEVER push the PCA button for the patient — the safety mechanism is that ONLY the patient presses it, preventing overdose.

column1: What is the drug classification of acetaminophen?
column2:
Analgesic, Antipyretic

Acetaminophen relieves pain and reduces fever. It is NOT an anti-inflammatory (not an NSAID).

column1: What is the drug classification of acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), ibuprofen, and ketorolac?
column2:
NSAID — Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug: Analgesic, Antipyretic, Anti-inflammatory

NSAIDs have 3 effects: pain relief, fever reduction, AND anti-inflammation. Differ from acetaminophen which lacks the anti-inflammatory effect.

column1: What is the drug classification of codeine, oxycodone/acetaminophen, morphine sulfate, and hydromorphone?
column2:
Opiate Analgesic

Opiates bind to opioid receptors to relieve pain. All carry risk of respiratory depression, constipation, and dependence.

column1: What is the drug classification of naloxone?
column2:
Opiate Antagonist

Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid effects. Give when RR <10 after opioid administration.

column1: What is the drug classification of lidoderm (lidocaine)?
column2:
Local Anesthetic

Lidocaine blocks nerve conduction locally. Used for local pain relief without affecting consciousness.

column1: What is the drug classification of penicillin (ampicillin), gentamycin sulfate, and azithromycin?
column2:
Anti-infective

Anti-infectives fight bacterial infections. Used pre-op to reduce microbial burden and post-op to treat infections.

column1: What is the drug classification of midazolam and propofol?
column2:
Anesthetic Sedation. Midazolam (Versed) = anxiolytic, benzodiazepine, amnesiac. Propofol (Diprivan) = used for moderate sedation.

Midazolam causes amnesia — patients may not remember events during the procedure. Propofol has very rapid onset and offset.

column1: What is the drug classification of atropine sulfate?
column2:
Anticholinergic, Cardiac Agent

Atropine reduces oral and pulmonary secretions pre-op, decreasing the risk of aspiration pneumonia. Also used for bradycardia.

column1: What is the drug classification of docusate sodium?
column2:
Stool Softener

Docusate sodium (Colace) softens stool by drawing water into it. Used to prevent constipation in immobile or post-op patients.

column1: What is the drug classification of senna?
column2:
Laxative / Antacid

Senna stimulates intestinal motility. Often combined with docusate for opioid-induced constipation.

column1: What is the drug classification of polyethylene glycol?
column2:
Bulk-forming Fiber Laxative

Polyethylene glycol (MiraLax) draws water into the colon to soften and increase stool bulk. Often used for constipation from immobility.

column1: What is the drug classification of ondansetron?
column2:
Anti-emetic

Ondansetron (Zofran) prevents and treats nausea and vomiting. Used post-op to prevent aspiration pneumonia from vomiting.

column1: What is the drug classification of ascorbic acid and zinc?
column2:
Vitamins. Ascorbic acid = Vitamin C. Zinc = trace mineral/vitamin supplement.

Both ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) and zinc are essential for wound healing — collagen synthesis and immune function.
